title: Round four — the sheet, the action card, and four headers

steps.path: The sessions arrow at the top of the window, then Resume
steps.headline: Which header should the conversation get?
steps.notice: The two things you asked for are built and are the same in all four: the sheet, and the action card at the foot of it — model, folder and Resume sitting where the message box sits in a real conversation. Resume has left the header entirely, which is what makes room for the actions below.
steps.risk: All four offer the same three actions — rename, tags and note, mark complete — reaching them is the only difference. Tags and note open a panel under the header in every one of them.

variants.label: Two glyphs
variants.summary: The same tag and complete marks the card in the list already carries, at the size of a header. The name itself is the rename control — dotted underline and a pencil, exactly as on the card.
variants.risk: Two outlines and no words. Whoever has not learned what the tag shape means has to press it to find out.

variants.label: Everything is a pill
variants.summary: The tags it already has and the things you can do sit on one wrapping row: the applied tags, then Tag, Complete and Rename. Same pill shape as the filters on the other side of the window.
variants.risk: A conversation with five tags pushes the actions onto a second line, so the row's height moves around.

variants.label: A strip of words
variants.summary: Name and facts, then a strip beneath them spelling the actions out: Rename · Tags & note · Mark complete. Nothing to decode.
variants.risk: It costs a whole extra strip of height, on every conversation, whether or not you ever use it.

variants.label: One ⋯ button
variants.summary: The header stays purely the conversation — name, folder, date, size, tags — and a single ⋯ at the right holds all three actions.
variants.risk: Everything is one press further away, and ⋯ tells you nothing about what is inside until you open it.

steps.path: The card at the foot of the conversation
steps.headline: Where should Skip Permissions and Launch in New Window live on the action card?
steps.notice: The picture shows the ▾ opened. Model and folder are always on the card face; these two switches are what the ▾ hides.
steps.risk: The card grows upward when it opens and covers the last message. That is a rough edge in the draft, not a decision — it gets fixed whichever option wins.

options.label: Both behind the ▾
pros: The card stays one line, so the conversation keeps almost all the height.
The switches are still one press away when you want them.
cons: Skip Permissions is a switch that removes a safety check, and it is out of sight until you go looking.

options.label: Skip Permissions on the card face
pros: A switch that turns off a safety check is never hidden.
You can see the state of it before you press Resume, not after.
cons: The card becomes two lines tall on every Claude conversation, forever, for a switch most people leave alone.
options.cost: A second row on the card.

options.label: Not here at all
pros: The simplest card of the three: model, folder, Resume, done.
cons: The only way to resume with permissions skipped would be to change the app-wide default first.
options.cost: Removes a per-conversation choice that exists today.
